The WarpX collaboration has been successful due to its access to a number of funding sources from multiple funding offices, strong personalities leading the development who regularly reach out to users and partners, and multi-country interest in the success of the project leading to additional buy-in. Even with such strong support, there is concern within the project that the new funding model will not provide the resources necessary to continue development without stronger internal lab and funding agency support. Various industry entities are helping to increase usage of the tool by additional partners, but project leadership does not have a model in place to handle members who are not lab or academic. 4.1.3 Case Study: EPICS [8] The Experimental Physics and Industrial Control System (EPICS) is an ecosystem of software packages designed for distributed control of large facilities, such as particle accelerators. The framework is widely used, with a robust system of packages and interfaces. Most of the key interfaces and protocols were developed by specific individuals with interest in continuing project development, keeping the project alive. Government funding has generally been available for project-based support, but long-term funding has only been available on an ancillary basis, through individuals contributing their time. Project governance is multinational, with no single source of funding or development leadership. There are specific individuals, in particular Michael Davidsaver, Andrew Johnson, and Mark Rivers, who are key developers and provide project leadership in an ad hoc manner. While the project does have an official membership and leadership model, the lack of a single funding stream has led to several major components experiencing non-project-based development planning. An example of this can be seen in the development of the main GUI and interface tool, Control System Studio, that is now developed primarily by the European Spallation Source and ORNL, while the C++ and python libraries are generally developed by Argonne National Lab and Osprey DCS. This model leaves the project reliant on funding for specific individuals to introduce new features or maintain current systems, and would not be financially sustainable as an open source software ecosystem outside of the fact that the software has been deployed at a number of facilities that rely on it. Even so, many facilities are still using versions of the software developed 10 years ago, and the dual language (i.e. Java and C++) development paths can lead to bugs and features confusion. 16 Legally, code ownership and licensing is generally ambiguous, as was shown earlier in this discussion, with significant questions as to how other software packages integrate in with more standard licenses.
